paragraphs.modern: When Socrates had finished speaking, the company applauded. Aristophanes was starting to say something in answer to the allusion Socrates had made to his own speech, the one about lovers seeking their other half, when suddenly there was a loud knocking at the door of the house, as if a party of revelers had arrived, and the sound of a flute-girl could be heard. Agathon told the attendants to go and see who the intruders were. 'If they are friends of ours,' he said, 'invite them in; but if not, say that the drinking is over.' A little while later they heard the voice of Alcibiades ringing through the courtyard. He was very drunk, and kept roaring and shouting, 'Where is Agathon? Take me to Agathon!' At last, propped up by the flute-girl and some of his attendants, he found his way to them. 'Hail, friends,' he said, appearing at the door crowned with a massive garland of ivy and violets, with ribbons streaming from his head. 'Will you have a very drunk man as a companion in your revels? Or shall I just crown Agathon, which is what I came to do, and go away? I couldn't come yesterday, and that is why I am here today, with these ribbons on my head: I mean to take them off my own head and crown the head of the handsomest and wisest of men — if I may be allowed to call him that. Will you laugh at me because I'm drunk? Laugh if you like; I know very well that I am speaking the truth. But first tell me: if I come in, will you accept the terms I mentioned, and take me in as drunk as I am?
paragraphs.notes: The allusion is identified as Aristophanes' other-half story (Diotima's reference in ch. 7). Jowett's bracketed '(supra ...)' note is folded into 'take me in as drunk as I am'. The quote stays open because Alcibiades' speech continues into KEEP 8.1, which closes it.

paragraphs.modern: The company loudly begged him to take his place among them, and Agathon specially invited him. So he was led in by the people who were with him; and as he was being led in, intending to crown Agathon, he took the ribbons from his own head and held them in front of his eyes. This kept him from seeing Socrates, who made room for him, and Alcibiades took the empty place between Agathon and Socrates; and as he took the place, he embraced Agathon and crowned him. 'Take off his sandals,' said Agathon, 'and let him make a third on the same couch.'

'By all means; but who is the third partner in our revels?' said Alcibiades, turning round; and he jumped up as he caught sight of Socrates. 'By Heracles,' he said, 'what is this? Here is Socrates, always lying in wait for me, and always, as his way is, turning up in all sorts of unexpected places! And now, what have you got to say for yourself? And why are you lying here, where, I notice, you have managed to find a place not next to a joker or lover of jokes, like Aristophanes, but next to the best-looking person here?'

Socrates turned to Agathon and said: 'I must ask you to protect me, Agathon, because this man's passion has become quite a serious matter for me. Ever since I became his admirer, I have never been allowed to talk to anyone else good-looking, or so much as look at them. If I do, he goes wild with envy and jealousy; he not only insults me but can barely keep from hitting me, and at this very moment he may do me some harm. Please see to this: either reconcile me with him, or, if he turns violent, protect me, because I am in physical fear of his mad and passionate attacks.'

'There can never be any reconciliation between you and me,' said Alcibiades, 'but for now I'll put off punishing you. And I must ask you, Agathon, to give me back some of the ribbons, so that I can crown the marvelous head of this universal despot. I don't want him complaining that I crowned you and neglected him, when in conversation he is the conqueror of all mankind — and not just once, as you were the day before yesterday, but always.' Then, taking some of the ribbons, he crowned Socrates, and lay down again.

'That is good, Eryximachus,' said Alcibiades, 'and yet it is hardly fair to compare a drunk man's speech with the speeches of sober men. And I should like to know, sweet friend, whether you really believe what Socrates was saying just now. I can assure you that the exact opposite is true, and that if I praise anyone but him in his presence, whether god or man, he will hardly be able to keep from hitting me.'
'Well then,' said Eryximachus, 'praise Socrates, if you like.'

'Then I will begin at once,' said Alcibiades, 'and if I say anything that is not true, you may interrupt me if you like and say, "That is a lie," though my intention is to speak the truth. But don't be surprised if I jump around, saying things as they come into my head, because listing all your oddities smoothly and in order is not an easy task for a man in my condition.
paragraphs.notes: No closing quote: Alcibiades' speech runs straight on into 8.23 (glossary multi-paragraph rule). The current text closed it here and reopened at 8.23.

paragraphs.modern: 'And now, my boys, I shall praise Socrates by means of an image, which he will take for a caricature; but I am not using it to make fun of him, only for the sake of the truth. I say that he is exactly like the busts of Silenus, the pot-bellied old satyr, that you see set up in the sculptors' shops, holding pipes and flutes in their mouths. They are hollow and made to open down the middle, and inside them are images of gods. I say also that he is like Marsyas the satyr, the legendary flute-player. You yourself won't deny, Socrates, that your face looks like a satyr's. Yes, and you resemble them in other ways too. For example, you are insolent, as I can prove with witnesses, if you won't confess it. And aren't you a flute-player? You certainly are, and a far more wonderful performer than Marsyas. He, it is true, used instruments to charm people's souls with the power of his breath, and anyone who plays his music still does so today. For the melodies of Olympus, Marsyas's pupil, come from Marsyas, who taught them to him; and these melodies, whether a great master plays them or a second-rate flute-girl, have a power that no others have. They alone take possession of the soul, and they reveal which listeners are in need of the gods and their secret rites, because the melodies themselves are divine. But you produce the same effect with words alone, without needing a flute. That is the difference between you and him.
paragraphs.notes: Opens Alcibiades' multi-paragraph speech; not closed (it ends at 8.38). 'Busts' kept, to match 'opens the bust' in 8.37. 'Insolent' for Jowett's 'bully'.

paragraphs.modern: 'When we hear any other speaker, even a very good one, he has absolutely no effect on us, or not much; but mere fragments of you and your words, even at second hand, and however badly repeated, amaze and possess the souls of every man, woman, and child who hears them. And if I weren't afraid you would think me hopelessly drunk, I would swear on oath, and not just tell you, what an effect your words have always had on me, and still have. For when I hear them, my heart leaps inside me even more than the hearts of the Corybantian revelers — those worshipers who dance in a religious frenzy — and my eyes rain tears. And I see that many others are affected in the same way. I have heard Pericles and other great orators, and I thought they spoke well, but I never felt anything like this; my soul was not stirred by them, nor was I angry at the thought of my own slavish state. But this Marsyas here has often driven me to the point where I felt I could hardly bear to go on living the life I lead — this, Socrates, you will admit. And I know that if I did not stop my ears against him and flee, as from the Sirens' song, the same thing would happen to me as to others: he would hold me transfixed, and I would grow old sitting at his feet. For he makes me confess that I ought not to live as I do, neglecting the needs of my own soul and busying myself with the affairs of the Athenians. So I hold my ears and tear myself away from him.
paragraphs.notes: Opening quote added per the glossary multi-paragraph rule (the current text had none). KEEP 8.25 still lacks one.

paragraphs.modern: 'And this is what I and many others have suffered from the flute-playing of this satyr. But hear me once more, while I show you how exact the image is, and how marvelous his power. For let me tell you, none of you knows him; but I will reveal him to you. Having begun, I must go on. Do you see how he is drawn to beautiful young men? He is always around them, always being smitten by them; and then again, he knows nothing and is ignorant of everything. That is the appearance he puts on. Isn't he like a Silenus in this? Of course he is. His outer mask is the carved head of the Silenus; but, my fellow drinkers, when he is opened up, what self-control you find inside! Believe me, beauty and wealth and honor, which most people marvel at, count for nothing with him; he utterly despises them. He does not care at all about the people who have them; human beings are nothing to him; he spends his whole life mocking and scorning them. But when I opened him up and looked inside at his serious purpose, I saw in him divine and golden images of such fascinating beauty that I was ready to do in a moment whatever Socrates commanded. Others may not have noticed them, but I saw them. Now, I imagined that he was seriously in love with my beauty, and I thought this would give me a grand opportunity to hear him tell me everything he knew; for I had a wonderfully high opinion of my youthful charms.

'To carry out this plan, the next time I went to see him I sent away the attendant who usually came with me. I will confess the whole truth, and I beg you to listen; and if I say anything false, you, Socrates, must expose it. Well, he and I were alone together, and I thought that now, with nobody else there, I would hear him speak to me the way a lover speaks to his beloved when they are alone, and I was delighted. Nothing of the sort. He talked with me as usual, spent the day with me, and then went away. Next I challenged him to a match at the wrestling school, and he wrestled and grappled with me several times with no one else there; I imagined I might get somewhere that way. Not a bit of it; I got nowhere with him. Finally, since I had failed so far, I thought I must take stronger measures and go after him boldly: since I had started, I would not give up on him, but would find out how matters stood between him and me. So I invited him to dinner, just as if our roles were reversed and he were the handsome youth and I the older lover with designs on him. He was not easily persuaded to come, but after a while he did accept the invitation. The first time he came, he wanted to leave as soon as dinner was over, and I didn't have the nerve to keep him. The second time, still following my plan, I went on talking with him after dinner far into the night, and when he wanted to go, I made the excuse that it was late and that he had much better stay.
paragraphs.notes: Role reversal made explicit ('as if our roles were reversed'). 'Challenged him to a match at the wrestling school' keeps Jowett's 'challenged'.

paragraphs.modern: 'So he lay down on the couch next to me, the same couch he had reclined on at dinner, and no one but the two of us was sleeping in the room. All this could be told to anyone without shame. But what comes next I could hardly tell you if I were sober. Still, as the proverb says, "In vino veritas": in wine there is truth. Another saying has it that wine and children both tell the truth; so wine tells the truth with children or without them, and therefore I must speak. Nor, again, would it be right for me to hide the lofty conduct of Socrates when I have set out to praise him. What's more, I have felt the serpent's bite; and a man who has been bitten, as they say, is willing to talk about it only to his fellow sufferers, because they alone are likely to understand him, and will not judge too harshly the things his agony drove him to say or do. For I have been bitten by something worse than a viper. In my soul, or in my heart, or in some other part of me, I have known the worst pang of all, which bites a gifted young mind more painfully than any serpent's tooth: the pang of philosophy, which will make a man say or do anything. And all of you I see around me — Phaedrus and Agathon and Eryximachus and Pausanias and Aristodemus and Aristophanes, and I need not mention Socrates himself — all of you have experienced the same madness and passion in your longing for wisdom. So listen, and forgive what I did then and what I am saying now. But, as at the sacred mysteries, let the attendants and anyone else who is uninitiated or ill-mannered close up the doors of their ears.
paragraphs.notes: The double proverb is spelled out: 'in vino veritas' plus 'wine and children tell the truth'. It uses 'children', not Jowett's 'boys', because in this passage 'boys' would read as lovers. The proverb is a quotation inside speech, so it takes double quotes.

paragraphs.modern: 'When the lamp was put out and the servants had gone away, I thought I must speak plainly to him and put an end to the ambiguity. So I gave him a shake and said, "Socrates, are you asleep?" "No," he said. "Do you know what I have in mind?" "What do you have in mind?" he said. "I think," I replied, "that of all the admirers I have ever had, you are the only one who is worthy of me, and you seem too modest to speak up. Now, I feel that I would be a fool to refuse you this or any other favor, and so I have come to lay at your feet everything I have and everything my friends have, in the hope that you will help me along the way of virtue. That is what I desire above all things, and I believe you can help me in it better than anyone else. And I would certainly be more ashamed of what wise men would say if I refused a favor to a man like you than of what the world, which is mostly fools, would say about me if I granted it." He answered in the ironic manner that is so characteristic of him: "Alcibiades, my friend, you are aiming high indeed, if what you say is true, and if there really is some power in me that can make you better. You must see in me some rare beauty, of a kind infinitely higher than any I see in you. So if you mean to share with me and exchange beauty for beauty, you will get much the better of the bargain: you will gain true beauty in return for the appearance of beauty — like Diomede in Homer, who got gold armor in exchange for bronze.
paragraphs.notes: The bedroom dialogue is nested inside Alcibiades' speech, so it switches to double quotes (glossary). 'Have in mind' replaces 'meditating' and covers both thought and intent. Socrates' reply runs on into 8.30.

paragraphs.modern: '"But look again, sweet friend, and see whether you are not mistaken about me. The mind's eye begins to see sharply when the body's eyes begin to fail, and you have a long way to go before you are old." When I heard this, I said, "I have told you what I intend, and I am entirely serious. Now you decide what you think is best for you and me." "That is good," he said. "Some other time, then, we will think it over and do what seems best, about this and about other matters." At that, I imagined he was smitten, and that the words I had let fly like arrows had wounded him. So, without waiting to hear more, I got up, threw my coat around him, and crept under his threadbare cloak, since it was winter; and there I lay the whole night with this wonderful monster, this extraordinary being, in my arms. You won't deny this either, Socrates. And yet, in spite of everything, he was so unmoved by my advances, so contemptuous and mocking and disdainful of my beauty — which I really thought had some attractions! Hear me, judges, for you shall be the judges of Socrates' haughty virtue: nothing more happened. When I woke up in the morning — let all the gods and goddesses be my witnesses — I got up as if I had been sleeping beside my father or an elder brother.
paragraphs.notes: The paragraph opens with both marks because Socrates' nested reply continues from 8.29. Jowett's broken sentence becomes an exclamation, then the appeal to the judges, then 'nothing more happened'.

paragraphs.modern: 'What do you suppose I felt after this rejection, at the thought of my own humiliation? And yet I couldn't help marveling at his natural self-control and restraint and manliness. I never imagined I could meet a man like him, with such wisdom and endurance. So I could not be angry with him or give up his company, any more than I could hope to win him. For I knew very well that money could wound him even less than steel could wound the great warrior Ajax; and the one way I had of capturing him, my good looks, had failed. So I was at my wit's end; no one was ever more hopelessly enslaved by another. All this happened before he and I went on the campaign at Potidaea, the northern city that Athens was besieging. There we shared the army's mess, and I had the chance to observe his extraordinary power of enduring fatigue. His endurance was simply marvelous when we were cut off from our supplies and forced to go without food. On such occasions, which often happen in war, he outdid not only me but everyone; there was no one to compare with him. Yet at a festival he was the only one who could really enjoy himself. He didn't want to drink, but if he was made to, he could beat us all at it; and, amazingly, no human being had ever seen Socrates drunk. And if I'm not mistaken, his powers will be tested before long. His toughness in enduring the cold was also surprising.
paragraphs.notes: The Ajax comparison is unpacked, and Potidaea gets a few words of context. 'Wit's end' matches KEEP 8.25.

paragraphs.modern: while he was on the expedition. One morning he was thinking about something he could not resolve. He would not give it up, but went on thinking from early dawn until noon; there he stood, fixed in thought. At noon people began to notice him, and the rumor ran through the wondering crowd that Socrates had been standing there thinking about something ever since daybreak. At last, in the evening after supper, some Ionians, out of curiosity — I should explain that this was not in winter but in summer — brought out their mats and slept in the open air so that they could watch him and see whether he would stand there all night. He stood there until the following morning; and when the light returned, he offered up a prayer to the sun and went his way. I will also tell you, if you like — and indeed I am bound to tell you — about his courage in battle; for who but he saved my life? This was the battle in which I received the prize for valor: I was wounded, and he would not leave me, but rescued both me and my weapons. And it was he who ought to have received the prize for valor, which the generals wanted to give me, partly because of my rank; and I told them so — this, again, Socrates will not dispute or deny — but he was more eager than the generals that I, and not he, should have the prize.
paragraphs.notes: No opening quote: the paragraph continues mid-sentence from KEEP 8.33 through the Homer line in 8.34. Plato's own parenthetical asides are set off with spaced dashes, so no brackets remain.

paragraphs.modern: 'There was another occasion when his behavior was very remarkable: during the army's flight after our defeat at the battle of Delium, where he served in the heavy infantry. I had a better opportunity of seeing him there than at Potidaea, because I was on horseback myself, and therefore comparatively out of danger. He and the general Laches were retreating, since the troops were in flight, and I met them, told them not to lose heart, and promised to stay with them. And there you could see him, Aristophanes, just as you portray him in your comedy The Clouds, and just as he is in the streets of Athens: stalking like a pelican and rolling his eyes, calmly surveying enemies as well as friends, and making it obvious to anyone, even from a distance, that whoever attacked him would be likely to meet with stout resistance. That is how he and his companion got away. For in war this is the sort of man who is never touched; the only ones who get pursued are those running away headlong. I particularly noticed how much more presence of mind he had than Laches. I could tell of many marvels in praise of Socrates. Most of his ways might perhaps be matched in another man, but his absolute unlikeness to any human being who is alive now or who has ever lived is perfectly astonishing.
paragraphs.notes: Restores the Clouds reference that was lost with Jowett's note. 'Our defeat' gives the few words of context Delium needs.

paragraphs.modern: 'You might imagine that the Spartan general Brasidas and others were like Achilles; or you might imagine that Nestor and Antenor, Homer's wise old counselors, were like the statesman Pericles; and the same may be said of other famous men. But you will never be able to find any likeness to this strange being, however remote, either among men who live now or among those who have ever lived — other than the one I have already suggested, Silenus and the satyrs. They are an image not only of him, but of his words. For, although I forgot to mention this before, his words are like those Silenus busts that open up. When you first hear them, they sound ridiculous. He wraps himself in language like the skin of a wanton satyr: he talks about pack-donkeys and blacksmiths and cobblers and leather-workers, and he is always saying the same things in the same words, so that any ignorant or inexperienced person might feel inclined to laugh at him. But anyone who opens the bust and sees what is inside will find that his are the only words with any meaning in them, and also the most divine, full of beautiful images of virtue, and of the widest scope — or rather, reaching to the whole duty of a good and honorable man.

'That, my friends, is my praise of Socrates. I have also added my blame of him, for the way he has mistreated me; and he has mistreated not only me but Charmides the son of Glaucon, and Euthydemus the son of Diocles, and many others in the same way. He starts out as their lover, the older man courting them, and ends up with them courting him instead. So I tell you, Agathon: "Don't be deceived by him. Learn from me and take warning, and don't be like the fool in the proverb, who learns only by getting hurt."'
paragraphs.notes: Closes Alcibiades' speech that opened at 8.23. The proverb is the 'fool learns by suffering' saying.

paragraphs.modern: When Alcibiades had finished, there was laughter at his frankness, because he seemed to be still in love with Socrates. 'You are sober, Alcibiades,' said Socrates, 'or you would never have gone to such roundabout lengths to hide the purpose of all this praise of your satyr. For this whole long story is just an ingenious detour, and its real point is slipped in at the end as if in passing: you want to stir up a quarrel between me and Agathon. Your idea is that I ought to love you and nobody else, and that you, and you only, ought to love Agathon. But the plot of this satyr play of yours — this Silenus drama, like the bawdy comic pieces staged after the tragedies — has been found out, and you must not let him, Agathon, turn us against each other.'

'Certainly not,' said Socrates. 'Each of us is to praise his neighbor on the right. You have praised me, so now it is my turn to praise mine. If Agathon lay between us, he would be out of order, praising me again when he ought rather to be praised by me. So I must ask you to agree to this and not be jealous, for I have a great desire to praise the young man.'
paragraphs.notes: The seating rule from KEEP 8.13 is restated first so the step can be followed.

paragraphs.modern: 'The usual thing,' said Alcibiades. 'Wherever Socrates is, no one else has any chance with the good-looking young men. And now look how readily he has invented a specious reason for drawing Agathon to himself.'

Agathon was getting up to take a place on the couch beside Socrates when suddenly a crowd of revelers burst in, throwing the whole party into confusion. Someone leaving had left the front door open, and they poured in without ceremony. All order vanished, and everyone was forced to drink enormous quantities of wine. Aristodemus said that Eryximachus, Phaedrus, and some others left at that point, while he himself fell asleep and slept for a long time — the nights were long at that season. He woke near dawn, as the cocks were crowing, and saw that most of the company were either asleep or had gone. Only Agathon, Aristophanes, and Socrates were still awake, drinking from a large bowl that they passed around. Socrates was arguing with them. Aristodemus couldn't remember most of what was said — he'd missed the beginning and was still half asleep — but the gist was that Socrates was forcing them to admit that the gift for writing comedy was the same as the gift for writing tragedy, and that a true master of tragedy must also be a master of comedy. They were being compelled to agree, though they weren't entirely following the argument and kept nodding off. Aristophanes fell asleep first, and then, as daylight was breaking, Agathon. Socrates, having put them both to sleep, got up and left. Aristodemus followed him, as was his habit. Socrates went to the Lyceum, bathed, and spent the rest of the day as usual. In the evening, he went home to bed.
paragraphs.notes: Only the three assessor edits: removed 'The noise was tremendous' and 'from left to right', and restored Jowett's claim that the gift for comedy is the same as the gift for tragedy.
